This page is a reference for the algebra used in the homology calculation. It
contains only five ideas: coefficient fields, bases, matrices, kernels and
images, and quotients. Consult the linked section when one of those ideas is
unfamiliar; the main argument does not require reading this page from start to
finish.

## Scalars and fields {#coefficient-fields}

A **field** is an arithmetic system in which addition, subtraction and
multiplication are available, and every nonzero element can be divided by.
The rational, real and complex numbers are familiar fields. The integers are
not: for example, the integer 2 has no multiplicative inverse among the
integers.

A vector space is defined over a field because the field specifies which
scalars may be used in linear combinations. Homology can be computed with
several coefficient systems; using a field makes chain spaces and homology
vector spaces, so rank and dimension are available.

### The coefficient field $\mathbb F_2$

The first calculations use

$$
\mathbb F_2=\{0,1\},
\qquad 1+1=0.
$$

This is arithmetic modulo 2: only parity is retained. If 1 means “included”,
adding the same item twice returns to 0 because it has appeared an even number
of times. For chains, a simplex is therefore either present or absent, and
orientation signs disappear.

$\mathbb F_2$ is popular in TDA because binary arithmetic is exact and
efficient, and many first questions concern the presence of components, loops
or cavities rather than orientation. It is a modelling choice, not a neutral
default. Other fields can reveal different algebraic information. Integer
coefficients can also record torsion, but produce abelian groups rather than
vector spaces.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Other common coefficient choices"}
- $\mathbb F_p$ for prime $p$ uses arithmetic modulo $p$ and can expose
  prime-dependent behaviour.
- $\mathbb Q$ and $\mathbb R$ retain ordinary signs; for finite simplicial
  complexes they give the same Betti numbers.
- $\mathbb Z$ retains integral information, including torsion, but is not a
  field.
:::

## Vectors, span and bases {#vectors-and-bases}

The **span** of $v_1,\ldots,v_k$ contains every linear combination

$$
a_1v_1+\cdots+a_kv_k.
$$

A **basis** is an independent collection whose span is the whole vector
space. Every vector then has a unique coordinate column relative to that
basis. The dimension is the number of basis vectors.

The vector and its coordinate column are not the same object. In
$\mathbb R^2$, the vector $v=3e_1+e_2$ has coordinate column
$(3,1)^T$ in the standard Cartesian basis. A different basis gives different
coordinates for the same vector.

Order matters only when a basis is used for coordinates or matrix rows and
columns. Reordering a basis changes the coordinate bookkeeping, not the
underlying vector space.

**Why this appears in homology.** The $p$-simplices form a natural basis for
the chain space $C_p$. A chain is a vector in that space; its coordinate
column records the coefficient of each simplex.

## Linear maps and matrices {#linear-maps}

A **linear map** $T:V\to W$ preserves addition and scalar multiplication. Once
bases have been selected and ordered, a matrix $A$ represents that map:

$$
[T(v)]_C=A[v]_B.
$$

Each matrix column records the output of one input basis vector. For

$$
A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\2&2\end{pmatrix},
$$

both standard basis vectors are sent to $(1,2)^T$. The map $T$ is the
coordinate-independent object; $A$ is its description in the chosen bases.

**Why this appears in homology.** A boundary map is a linear map between chain
spaces. Its matrix columns record the boundaries of the basis simplices.

## Kernel, image, rank and nullity {#kernel-image}

For $T:V\to W$, the **kernel** and **image** are

$$
\ker T=\{v\in V:T(v)=0\},
\qquad
\operatorname{im}T=\{T(v):v\in V\}.
$$

The kernel contains input directions erased by the map. The image contains
the output directions the map can produce. Their dimensions are the nullity
and rank. For finite-dimensional $V$, rank-nullity states

$$
\dim V=\operatorname{rank}T+\operatorname{nullity}T.
$$

**Why this appears in homology.** For the boundary map $\partial_p$, the
kernel is the space of $p$-cycles. The image of $\partial_{p+1}$ is the space
of $p$-boundaries. Their dimensions determine the Betti number.

## Quotients {#quotients}

A **quotient** treats a specified kind of difference as irrelevant. This is
not ordinary division. Angles provide a familiar example: $0$, $2\pi$ and
$-2\pi$ are different real numbers but the same direction. Working modulo a
full turn groups them into one equivalence class.

**Why this appears in homology.** Two cycles represent the same homology class
when their difference is a boundary. The quotient

$$
H_p=Z_p/B_p
$$

retains cycles while deliberately forgetting differences supplied by
available fillings.

## Reading diagrams of maps {#reading-map-diagrams}

A diagram uses nodes for mathematical objects and arrows for maps. Read an
arrow from its source to its target. A square **commutes** when following
either directed route from one corner to the opposite corner produces the
same result.

This matters later when maps across filtration scale must be compatible. It
does not mean that the arrows are identical or invertible; it states that the
two compositions agree.

::: {.checkpoint-route}

The relevant reminders are:

1. a vector space has a stated coefficient field;
2. a basis gives coordinates but is not the underlying vector space;
3. a matrix represents a linear map in selected bases;
4. kernels contain erased inputs and images contain attainable outputs; and
5. a quotient identifies objects whose specified difference is being ignored.

:::
